label: rem:trace-locality-gs-non-locality
title: Gröbner–Shirshov reduction is non-local
html:
Let \beta = \sigma_{i_1} \cdots \sigma_{i_N} have Gröbner–Shirshov normal form \mathrm{NF}_{\mathrm{GS}}(\beta) = e_{j_1} \cdots e_{j_M}. Unlike the Markov locality of 7.3.7, the reduction to normal form is non-local. This is an informal observation; no precise statement of it is proved here.

The Gröbner–Shirshov reduction algorithm on the Hecke algebra applies three rewriting rules:

  • Hecke quadratic relation: \sigma_i^2 \to (q - q^{-1}) \sigma_i + 1 (eliminates squared generators).
  • Braid relation: \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \to \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} (Yang–Baxter / commutation).
  • Far-commutativity: \sigma_i \sigma_j \to \sigma_j \sigma_i for \lvert i - j \rvert \geq 2.

The braid relation acts on a window of three consecutive generators, and successive applications can propagate changes across the entire braid word. Therefore the normal form depends non-locally on the input — flipping a single generator in \beta can require rewriting many generators in \mathrm{NF}_{\mathrm{GS}}(\beta).

Reconciliation. Markov locality and this non-locality concern different operations. The first is a property of the trace and the second a property of the reduction to normal form, so they do not conflict: the composite \beta \mapsto \mathrm{tr}_M(\rho(\beta)) passes through the non-local map \beta \mapsto \mathrm{NF}_{\mathrm{GS}}(\beta), and the trace is then evaluated on the normal form.

Whether the trace of the normal form factorises over its letters is discussed in the product-factorisation check.
